cmo-cmo-1985-01.title: Reduce to a quadratic at each vertex
cmo-cmo-1985-01.body:
The triangle has perimeter $24$ and (being right-angled, $6^2 + 8^2 = 10^2$) area $\frac12\cdot6\cdot8 = 24$.

**Setting up.** A line that bisects the area divides the triangle into two pieces of positive area, so it meets the boundary in exactly two points $P$, $Q$ lying on two different sides (a point may be a vertex). Any two sides share a vertex $V$; let $P$ be on the side of length $b$ from $V$ and $Q$ on the side of length $c$ from $V$, with $p = VP \in (0, b]$, $q = VQ \in (0, c]$. One piece is the triangle $VPQ$; its share of the boundary is $p + q$ (plus the common cut $PQ$), so bisecting the perimeter means $p + q = 12$. If $\theta$ is the angle at $V$, bisecting the area means $\frac12 pq\sin\theta = \frac12\cdot\frac12 bc\sin\theta$, i.e. $pq = \frac{bc}{2}$. So $p, q$ are the roots of
$$t^2 - 12t + \frac{bc}2 = 0, \qquad t = 6 \pm \sqrt{36 - \tfrac{bc}{2}}.$$
Conversely, any such $p, q$ in the allowed ranges give a line bisecting both. We check the three vertices.

* **Vertex between sides $6$ and $8$** ($bc/2 = 24$): $t = 6 \pm 2\sqrt3 \approx 9.46,\ 2.54$. The larger root exceeds both $6$ and $8$, so it fits on neither side. No line.
* **Vertex between sides $8$ and $10$** ($bc/2 = 40$): $36 - 40 < 0$, no real roots. No line.
* **Vertex between sides $6$ and $10$** ($bc/2 = 30$): $t = 6 \pm \sqrt6 \approx 8.45,\ 3.55$. The root $6 + \sqrt6 > 6$ cannot lie on the side of length $6$, so necessarily $p = 6 - \sqrt6$ on the side $6$ and $q = 6 + \sqrt6 \le 10$ on the side $10$. Exactly one line.

Every bisecting line arises in this way from (at least) one vertex, and only one candidate survives (it does not pass through a vertex, so it is not counted twice). Hence there is exactly one line bisecting both the area and the perimeter. ∎

cmo-cmo-1985-02.title: Write the number in terms of its first digit
cmo-cmo-1985-02.body:
We **disprove** it (apart from the trivial $0 = 2\cdot 0$; signs do not matter, since moving digits of $-N$ is the same as for $N$, so we take $N > 0$).

Let $N$ have $k + 1$ digits with first digit $a \in \{1, \dots, 9\}$, so $N = a\cdot10^k + m$ with $0 \le m < 10^k$ ($m$ is the number formed by the remaining $k$ digits, possibly with leading zeros). Moving the first digit to the end gives $10m + a$. The condition is
$$10m + a = 2(a\cdot10^k + m) \iff 8m = a\,(2\cdot10^k - 1).$$
* If $k = 0$, then $m = 0$ and $a = 0$, impossible.
* If $k \ge 1$, the number $2\cdot10^k - 1$ is odd, so $8 \mid a$, i.e. $a = 8$. Then $m = 2\cdot10^k - 1 \ge 10^k$, contradicting $m < 10^k$.

So no positive integer is doubled when its initial digit is moved to the end. ∎

cmo-cmo-1985-03.title: Half-angle tangent
cmo-cmo-1985-03.body:
Let $r$ be the radius of the circle, $c = 2\pi r$, $n = 1985$ and $\theta = \frac{\pi}{n}$.

$P_1$ is circumscribed about the circle: each side subtends the angle $2\theta$ at the centre and touches the circle at its midpoint, so each side has length $2r\tan\theta$ and $x = 2nr\tan\theta$. $P_2$ is inscribed in the circle: each side is a chord subtending $2\theta$, of length $2r\sin\theta$, so $y = 2nr\sin\theta$. Since $2c = 4\pi r = 4nr\theta$, we must show
$$\tan\theta + \sin\theta \ge 2\theta.$$
Put $t = \tan\frac\theta2 \in (0, 1)$. The half-angle formulas give $\tan\theta = \frac{2t}{1-t^2}$ and $\sin\theta = \frac{2t}{1+t^2}$, so
$$\tan\theta + \sin\theta = 2t\left(\frac{1}{1-t^2} + \frac{1}{1+t^2}\right) = \frac{4t}{1 - t^4} \ge 4t.$$
By the given fact applied to $\frac\theta2 \in [0, \frac\pi2)$, $t = \tan\frac\theta2 \ge \frac\theta2$, hence $4t \ge 2\theta$. Combining, $\tan\theta + \sin\theta \ge 2\theta$, and multiplying by $2nr$:
$$x + y = 2nr(\tan\theta + \sin\theta) \ge 4nr\theta = 2c.$$
(In fact the inequality is strict, since $\frac{4t}{1-t^4} > 4t$ for $t > 0$.) ∎

cmo-cmo-1985-04.title: Legendre's formula in binary
cmo-cmo-1985-04.body:
Let $v(n)$ be the exponent of $2$ in $n!$. By Legendre's formula (each multiple of $2^i$ up to $n$ contributes one factor $2$ for each $i$ with $2^i$ dividing it),
$$v(n) = \sum_{i \ge 1}\left\lfloor \frac{n}{2^i}\right\rfloor.$$
Write $n$ in binary, $n = \sum_{j \ge 0} b_j2^j$ with $b_j \in \{0, 1\}$, and let $s(n) = \sum_j b_j$ be the number of binary ones. Then $\left\lfloor n/2^i\right\rfloor = \sum_{j \ge i} b_j 2^{j-i}$, so
$$v(n) = \sum_{j\ge 0} b_j\left(2^{j-1} + 2^{j-2} + \cdots + 1\right) = \sum_j b_j\,(2^j - 1) = n - s(n).$$
Now $2^{n-1} \mid n!$ means $v(n) \ge n - 1$, i.e. $s(n) \le 1$. Since $n \ge 1$ has $s(n) \ge 1$, this means $s(n) = 1$, i.e. $n$ has a single binary one: $n = 2^{k-1}$ for some positive integer $k$. Both directions follow from this chain of equivalences. ∎
